mutations.because: `comment` is not a field of `AddCommentPayload`. The payload carries `commentEdge`, and `IssueCommentEdge` carries `node`, so the url is three levels down — which is why this ran for a month against a schema that rejects it: GitHub refuses the WHOLE mutation document over one unknown selection, so the write that was supposed to post the class comment and resolve every thread posted nothing, resolved nothing, and reported a refusal the operator had to read as a permissions problem. Nothing else in the suite notices, and that is the part worth saying: the fetch-and-reader tests answer their own fixtures, so the reader and the mutation can be wrong in the same direction and stay green together — a test that feeds `addComment { comment { url } }` to a reader that reads `.comment.url` proves only that they agree. What catches it is the offline shape test, which asks the introspected schema whether `AddCommentPayload` declares the field the mutation names, and can fail with no network and no gh

mutations.because: a bare object field is refused by GitHub with 'Field must have selections', and the refusal takes the whole mutation document down — the same total loss as asking for a field that does not exist: the class comment posts nothing and not one thread resolves, and the operator is left reading a refusal. The anchor is the resolve template rather than the bare `thread`, because the template is what carries the set of id and isResolved; and it is worth a mutation of its own because the first one in this manifest only proved the walk can name a field, which a walk that never looks at selection sets is free to do — `thread` is a real field of ResolveReviewThreadPayload, so every field-existence check in the file still passes with the set gone. What catches it is the rule added beside the field lookup: whether a field carries a selection set is read from whether its introspected type is an object, so PullRequestReviewThread with no set is named in the failure the test prints
